questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: For a long time I've been interested in trying to live in Paris, since I love France and especially Paris. Furthermore, I would like France to be part of a major part of my future career, which was probably the most important aspect of my decision to spend a semester in Paris as an Erasmus student.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: While there was major differences from UCPH as far as the methods of teaching, for me the most important part of the semester was without a doubt the social aspect. I had received many "warnings" from other students I had contacted in connection with my considerations of studying in Paris, and other travel reports that mentioned the French students being very cold, the teaching system being too rigid and overall bad experiences. It made me a bit hesitative about spending a semester in Paris, however I knew that it had been my dream, and that I had to try it for myself and make my own experiences. Upon arrival and throughout the semester, I've made countless friends, French as well as other Erasmus students from Italy, Belgium, and more. I don't doubt that I will stay in contact with the friends I've made in Paris, since we connected very easily and we had lots of fun experiences on and off campus.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There was an information meeting in the end of august before classes started, where all the Erasmus students met each other and were shown around on the campus by French students afterwards. During this meeting, pretty much all concerns and questions I had were answered throughout the day. Overall, it was quite easy to find the information I needed upon arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a coordinator in charge of handling questions from international students throughout the whole semester. This person was present at the information meeting and made sure that all the Erasmus students felt at home and were not confused. Although I wasn't in really in a position where I needed much assistance, it was possible to get this if necessary.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It was nice to get shown around by the French students afterwards who were extremely open and welcoming.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: A couple months before leaving for Paris, I contacted a person I knew from the UCPH Law Faculty which I knew had spent a semester in Paris as Erasmus student, and this person got me in contact with the landlord who eventually rented me her apartment throughout the semester. Thus, very easily. It showed me how much your network can help you when looking for housing as an Erasmus student.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The rent in Paris is extremely expensive. The more in the center of Paris, the worse it gets. I was very happy with my apartment and liked to have my "own" place to live, however I highly recommend to apply for a room at La Fondation Danoise in the Cité Universitaire. Here you live with other Danes and other Europeans with a relatively cheap rent, in general at least much cheaper than renting an apartment.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Since I wanted to ensure that I had an apartment in Paris in case that the landlord scammed me, I also applied for a room through the university. However, there was no more rooms available.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was registered in the courses I had chosen without having to do anything myself, other than contacting the Erasmus-coordinator.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I was automatically registered in the courses that I had chosen in my Learning Agreement. Throughout the first couple of weeks I changed 1 course which was extremely easy, I just updated the Learning Agreement and sent it to UCPH and UPC. Thereafter, I was registered in the new course.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus Coordinator from UPC was (mostly) very helpful, although it sometimes took a very long time for her to answer compared to UCPH. I rarely had questions, so instead of e-mailing her, I just went to her office on campus.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Talk directly to the Erasmus-coordinator if you have questions and otherwise just remember to have a Learning Agreement containing the courses you want to follow. The last date to change the Learning Agreement was October 15th, so if you are in doubt, try the different courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: This is the part that would keep me from going to UPC, if I wanted a "relaxing" exchange semester without academic challenges. The courses, from L1 (first year of their "bachelor") to M1 (1st year of masters), were extremely challenging. What I've learned throughout the semester is in my view incomparable to anything I've tried at UCPH, which I'm also extremely grateful for.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Other than the fact that legal French is of course quite different than everyday French, the content of the courses was on a surprisingly high level. The best example I have of this, is the course "Introduction au marché intérieur européen", a M1 course of 3,5 ECTS. In this course, we were taught pretty much the same as in the 2nd year BA-course "EU-ret" on UCPH. However, the course also contained EU-competition law (including EU-merger control) and EU-state aid regulation. In my view, this tendency was also the case throughout the other courses I followed. In addition to the difficulty of the courses, if you ask me, 30 ECTS in UPC is not equivalent to 30 ECTS in UCPH. It was not possible to take a master's course with more than 3,5 ECTS, which motivated me to take some licence (bachelor's) courses of 6 ECTS. Their grading-system is also fundamentally different. In certain courses, obtaining a 10/20, which is necessary to pass the course, is not at all an easy task, and I witnessed many of my fellow French students fail courses, since they (contrary to at UCPH) need an average grade of 10/20 out of all the courses they've taken throughout the semester in order to pass. My impression was that it depends on the professor, and if this person is easier on the Erasmus students. There is definitely courses where this is the case, but also the opposite. 

Important note : The level of French (grammar etc.) in the classes is incredibly high, so I would at least say that you should be very, very comfortable in everyday French. In my case, I was required to take a DELF B2 test from home which cost around 1300DKK.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is important to note that the courses of 6 ECTS were TD courses, comparable to "seminartimer" at UCPH, thus both lectures and smaller classes. Presence and homework for these courses was not mandatory, and I didn't make homework for any of the 3 TD-courses I had, since this would require incredible amounts of time. As mentioned, I prioritized the social aspects of my exchange semester and didn't always meet up to all my classes. I would however say that one of the most interesting/bizarre experiences was the TD-classes. The amount of respect (fear) from the French students towards the TD-professor was something I have never experienced, probably since their grades depended on their performance in the TD-classes (not the case for Erasmus-students). This sometimes lead to small clashes between me and one professor since she didn't know the rules for Erasmus students were different. At least I found that the teaching style and institutional differences herein between Denmark and France are incredibly noticeable, but not necessarily negatively. The exams varied a lot, as I had both oral exams, written exams and a multiple choice.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Introduction générale au droit (6 ECTS), Introduction au droit constitutionnel (6 ECTS), Droit civil des contrats (6 ECTS), Droit de l'environnement (3,5 ECTS), Droit du marché intérieur européen (3,5 ECTS), Droit des sociétés commerciales (3,5 ECTS) and Histoire du droit des affaires et des relations sociales (3,5 ECTS) - in total 32 ECTS

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Since the system for TD courses is different and more lenient for Erasmus students, I would definitely recommend taking these in order to minimize the necessary amount of courses (and exams). Nevertheless, if you're interested in corporate law, I can highly recommend "Droit des sociétés commerciales" since this course thoroughly covers almost everything relevant as regards commercial company law in France.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Eating out can become very costly, and even though there are is an incredible amount of delicious cheap foods (banh mi and falafel especially), most of the bistros/brasseries are not very cheap.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Books and travel. I highly recommend renting a Swapfiets which costs 19 euros a month and takes you all over Paris. My travel expenses were higher due to sometimes taking the metro.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you wanted to, you could easily join sport clubs etc. However, unfortunately there was no possibilities for the sport I play, so I didn't participate in the sports offered. If I could do anything different, I would have joined of of these.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Many different associations, although I think these were in general for the French students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the museums, drink lots of wine, eat lots of cheese, experience the parks, the bars, the nightlife and the shops. Since Paris is undoubtedly the greatest city in the world for "la kiffance", this is what I enjoyed doing the most. Live life !

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I went to Normandy and Marseille on weekend trips, and especially Marseille is one of the most beautiful cities I've seen in Europe. The people there were unbelievably nice and open - I highly recommend going see some French cities and regions outside of Paris in the weekends.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Extremely easy. As long as you're open and actively trying to make friends with the students on campus, from your classes etc., it is very smooth. Even if French isn't your mother tongue, French students are not at all (at least regarding this) judgy. People are very friendly, however I would imagine that it is quite difficult making friends if you are not actively trying to speak to the local students. Even if you are nervous about your French, be brave and everything will be alright.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't be afraid, the local students were (almost) all extremely nice and friendly. Speak to the French students that show the Erasmus students around on campus, and you will quickly know many people on campus. Also, just saying hi and having conversations with the people next to you during the lectures was great for me.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Since it is quite a prestigeous university, the French students were super focused on their grades, which is not necessarily a cultural difference from UCPH, but it is nice to know. The waiters can often be rude.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I love the openness of French people as they were always open to share notes, talk, eat lunch, hang out etc. This is the main reason that I wouldn't have chosen any other university looking back now.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. Be prepared to work (the exam period was horrible hahah), 2. Always be open, 3. Enjoy as much as you can of Europe's cultural capital.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Applying for grants (legater) is extremely recommended. In my case, it drastically changed my exchange semester, as I had so much more financial freedom. Although it takes time, there is so many grants to apply for, and also French-specific grants as well.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I've made along the way and all that I've learned thanks to the courses. Additionally, just the experience of living in Paris is something that cannot be described.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Probably the exam period. 7 exams that were all extremely difficult made for a long and difficult exam period, even worse than at UCPH in my experience. However, the public libraries (especially la BnF) are easily accessible and incredibly beautiful.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Never be scared to ask for help from anyone, in my view it helps much more than I would have known

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
